english.heading: Seeds and Seed Sovereignty
body: Seed is where the next season begins.
When your household can save, store and share good seed, it carries more than a crop forward. It also carries the freedom to choose.
In this lesson, you will follow seed from the parent plant to the packet, the germination test and a neighbour’s hand.
Think about the crops in your area. Which ones do you already save seed from? Which seed do you buy? Which seed do you exchange?
Try to name at least one crop whose seed is already being saved in your area.

heading.text: Mbewu ni Vulawuri bya Mbewu (seed sovereignty)

body.text: Mbewu hi laha nguva leyi landzelaka yi sungulaka kona.
body.backTranslation: Seed is how the next time begins.

body.text: Loko ndyangu wa ka n'wina wu kota ku hlengeleta, ku hlayisa ni ku avelana mbewu leyinene, wu yisa swilo swo tala ku hundza ntshovelo ntsena. Wu tlhela wu yisa ntshunxeko wa ku hlawula.
body.backTranslation: When your family is able to gather, store and share good seed, it carries many things beyond the harvest only. It also carries the freedom to choose.

body.text: Eka dyondzo leyi, u ta landzelela mbewu ku suka eka ximilana xa mutswari ku ya eka xikwama, eka xikambelo xa ku mila, ni le voko ra muakelani.
body.backTranslation: In this lesson, you will follow the seed from the parent plant to the packet, to the germination test, and to the hand of the neighbour.

body.text: Anakanya hi swirimiwa (crops) swa le ndhawini ya ka n'wina. Hi swihi leswi mi se mi hlengeletaka mbewu ya swona? Hi yihi mbewu leyi mi yi xavaka? Hi yihi leyi mi yi cincanaka?
body.backTranslation: Think about the crops of your area. Which ones have you already gathered seed of? Which seed do you buy? Which do you swap?

body.text: Ringeta ku vula xirimiwa (crop) xin'we kumbe ku tlula lexi se ku hlengeletiwaka mbewu ya xona endhawini ya ka n'wina.
body.backTranslation: Try to name one crop or more than that whose seed has already been gathered in your area.

english.heading: Why Saving Seed Matters
body: Saving seed does not mean rejecting all bought seed. It means building practical choices.
Each crop you learn to save well removes one repeated purchase. It also begins a local record of what performs well in your soil and your season.
Think about the seed you buy again and again. Which repeated seed purchase costs your household the most each year?
Choose one crop from your planting list. Make it your practical starting point for seed saving. Do not try to save everything at once.

heading.text: Ha Yini Ku Hlengeleta Mbewu Swi Ri Swa Nkoka

body.text: Ku hlengeleta mbewu a swi vuli ku ala mbewu hinkwayo leyi xaviweke. Swi vula ku aka tindlela to tirhisiwa leti u nga ti hlawulaka.
body.backTranslation: Gathering seed does not mean refusing all bought seed. It means building methods to use that you choose.

body.text: Xirimiwa (crop) xin'wana ni xin'wana lexi u dyondzaka ku hlengeleta mbewu ya xona kahle xi susa ku xava kun'we loku phindha-phindhiwaka. Xi tlhela xi sungula rhekhodo ya le ndhawini ya ka n'wina ya leswi kulaka kahle emisaveni ya wena ni hi nguva ya wena.
body.backTranslation: Each crop whose seed you learn to gather well removes one repeated buying. It also begins a local record of what grows well in your soil and in your time.

body.text: Anakanya hi mbewu leyi u yi xavaka nkarhi ni nkarhi. Hi yihi mbewu leyi durhaka ngopfu ndyangu wa ka n'wina lembe rin'wana ni rin'wana?
body.backTranslation: Think about the seed that you buy time after time. Which seed is most expensive for your family each year?

body.text: Hlawula ximilana xin'we eka nxaxamelo wa wena wo byala. Xi endle ximilana xa wena xo sungula ku hlengeleta mbewu ya xona. U nga ringeti ku hlayisa swilo hinkwaswo hi nkarhi wun'we.
body.backTranslation: Choose one plant from your planting list. Make it your first plant to gather seed from. Do not try to store everything at the same time.

english.heading: Learning Outcomes
body: This lesson ends with a working seed store, not a list of facts.
You will make four decisions.
What will you save?
How will you process it?
How will you protect it?
And how will you know it is still alive before you depend on it?
Which of these four decisions is least familiar to you?
Say them again in your own words: select, process, protect and verify.

heading.text: Leswi U Nga Ta Swi Dyondza

body.text: Dyondzo leyi yi hela hi vuhlayiselo bya mbewu byo tirha, ku nga ri nxaxamelo wa timhaka ntsena.
body.backTranslation: This lesson ends with working seed storage, not only a list of matters.

body.text: U ta endla swiboho swa mune.
body.backTranslation: You will make four decisions.

body.text: U ta hlayisa yini?
body.backTranslation: What will you store?

body.text: U ta yi lulamisa hi ndlela yihi?
body.backTranslation: How will you prepare it?

body.text: U ta yi sirhelela hi ndlela yihi?
body.backTranslation: How will you protect it?

body.text: Naswona u ta swi tiva ku yini leswaku ya ha hanya u nga si yi tshemba?
body.backTranslation: And how will you know that it is still alive before you trust it?

body.text: Hi xihi eka swiboho leswi swa mune lexi u nga xi tolovelangiki ngopfu?
body.backTranslation: Which of these four decisions are you least used to?

body.text: Vula nakambe hi marito ya wena: hlawula, lulamisa, sirhelela, kutani u tiyisisa.
body.backTranslation: Say again in your own words: choose, prepare, protect, and then confirm.

english.heading: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed
body: Open-pollinated seed is not magic.
A stable variety can produce similar generations when it is properly isolated or self-pollinated.
F1 seed usually remains alive. But the next generation separates into different combinations of the parent traits.
The problem is unpredictability, not failure to germinate.
Think about one small bed on your own plot. Why could unpredictable plants be a risk when space is limited?
If you have seed packets, check whether they are marked open-pollinated or F1. Which would you choose for saving dependable seed?
Remember: the next F1 generation varies. It does not automatically die.

heading.text: Mbewu ya Open-Pollinated ni Mbewu ya F1

body.text: Mbewu ya open-pollinated a hi xihlamariso.
body.backTranslation: Open-pollinated seed is not a wonder/miracle.

body.text: Stable variety yi nga humesa switukulwana leswi fanaka loko yi hambanisiwe kahle (isolated) kumbe yi endla self-pollination.
body.backTranslation: A stable variety can/may produce generations that are alike when it has been separated well (isolated) or it does self-pollination.

body.text: Mbewu ya F1 hi ntolovelo yi ha hanya. Kambe xitukulwana lexi landzelaka xi hambana hi ku hlanganisiwa ka swihlawulekisi swa vatswari.
body.backTranslation: F1 seed usually still lives. But the next generation differs because of the mixing of the distinguishing features of the parents.

body.text: Xiphiqo hi ku nga tivekiki leswi swi nga ta humelela, ku nga ri ku tsandzeka ku mila (germinate).
body.backTranslation: The problem is in not knowing what will happen, not in failing to germinate.

body.text: Anakanya hi bedi rin'we ro tsongo ra ntanga ya wena. Ha yini swimilana leswi u nga tivi leswaku swi ta va njhani swi nga va khombo loko ndhawu yi ri yitsongo?
body.backTranslation: Think about one small bed of your garden. Why could plants that you do not know what they will be like be a danger when the place is small?

body.text: Loko u ri ni swikwama swa mbewu, languta loko swi tsariwile open-pollinated kumbe F1. U nga hlawula xihi ku hlayisa mbewu leyi tshembekaka?
body.backTranslation: When you have seed packets, look whether they are written open-pollinated or F1. Which can you choose to save seed that is trustworthy?

body.text: Tsundzuka: xitukulwana xa F1 lexi landzelaka xi hambana. A xi fi hi ku tisungulela.
body.backTranslation: Remember: the next F1 generation is different. It does not die by itself.

english.heading: Watch: Open-Pollinated Seed and F1 Seed
body: Watch both sides.
Both kinds of seed germinate.
Open-pollinated seed produces similar plants when the variety is stable and pollination is properly managed.
Seed saved from an F1 plant also germinates. But its next generation varies. Some plants may be tall. Others may be short. Their vigour and yield may differ.
Ask yourself what this means when choosing seed to save.
If you understand the difference, you can explain it in one sentence: both germinate, but the next F1 generation is unpredictable.

heading.text: Languta: Mbewu ya Open-Pollinated ni F1

body.text: Languta matlhelo hamambirhi.
body.backTranslation: Look at both sides.

body.text: Mbewu hamambirhi ya mila (germinate).
body.backTranslation: Both seeds germinate.

body.text: Mbewu ya open-pollinated yi humesa swimilana leswi fanaka loko muxaka (variety) wu ri stable ni loko pollination yi lawuriwa kahle.
body.backTranslation: Open-pollinated seed produces plants that are alike when the variety (variety) is stable and when pollination is controlled well.

body.text: Mbewu leyi hlayisiweke eka ximilana xa F1 na yona ya mila. Kambe xitukulwana xa yona lexi landzelaka xi hambana. Swimilana swin'wana swi nga leha. Swin'wana swi nga komba. Matimba ya swona ni ntshovelo wa swona swi nga hambana.
body.backTranslation: Seed stored from an F1 plant also germinates. But its next generation is different. Some plants may be tall. Others may be short. Their strength and their harvest may differ.

body.text: Tivutise leswaku leswi swi vula yini loko u hlawula mbewu leyi u nga ta yi hlayisa.
body.backTranslation: Ask yourself what this means when you choose seed that you will store.

body.text: Loko u twisisa ku hambana, u nga ku hlamusela hi xivulwa xin'we: hamambirhi ya mila, kambe xitukulwana xa F1 lexi landzelaka a xi tivekiki leswi xi nga ta va xiswona.
body.backTranslation: When you understand the difference, you can explain it in one saying: both germinate, but the next F1 generation is not known, what it will be.

english.heading: Seed Sovereignty
body: Seed sovereignty does not live in a slogan.
It lives in a dry packet, a written record and knowledge of how the seed behaves.
Your household begins it. Neighbours extend it. The seasons make the local seed collection more useful.
Which seed does your household already save best?
Draw a small map of the homes near you. Beside each home, write one crop that household could bring to a seed exchange.
Sovereignty needs three things: usable seed, written information and exchange.

heading.text: Vulawuri bya Mbewu (seed sovereignty)

body.text: Vulawuri bya mbewu (seed sovereignty) a byi hanyi eka xivulwa (slogan).
body.backTranslation: Seed sovereignty does not live in a slogan.

body.text: Byi hanya eka xikwama xo oma, rhekhodo leyi tsariweke ni vutivi bya ndlela leyi mbewu yi tikhomaka ha yona.
body.backTranslation: It lives in a dry packet, a written record, and knowledge of how the seed behaves.

body.text: Ndyangu wa ka n'wina wu wu sungula. Vaakelani va wu andzisa. Tinguva ta lembe ti endla leswaku mbewu leyi hlengeletiweke ya le ndhawini yi pfuna ku tlula loko yi sungula.
body.backTranslation: The family of your (pl.) home starts it. Neighbours increase it. The times of the year make it so that the seed that has been collected, of the place, helps to exceed when it starts.

body.text: Hi yihi mbewu leyi ndyangu wa ka n'wina se wu yi hlayisaka kahle ku tlula yin'wana ni yin'wana?
body.backTranslation: Which seed does your family already store well more than any other?

body.text: Dirowa mepe lowutsongo wa miti leyi nga kusuhi na wena. Etlhelo ka muti wun'wana ni wun'wana, tsala ximilana xin'we (crop) lexi ndyangu wolowo wu nga xi tiselaka ku cincana mbewu.
body.backTranslation: Draw a small map of the households that are near you. Beside each household, write one plant (crop) that that family brings for swapping seed.

body.text: Vulawuri byi lava swilo swinharhu: mbewu leyi nga tirhisiwaka, vuxokoxoko lebyi tsariweke ni ku cincana.
body.backTranslation: Sovereignty needs three things: seed that can be used, written details and swapping.

english.heading: Watch: Household Seed Network
body: Well-saved seed becomes more powerful when it is known and shared.
Watch one household begin by saving seed well from one crop. Dry seed goes into clean packets. Some packets move to neighbouring homes. The neighbours share different seed in return.
By the end, each household holds more varieties than it had before.
Think about which seed you could share and which seed you might receive from a neighbour. Seed moves. Knowledge and trust must move with it.

heading.text: Languta: Vuxaka bya Mbewu bya Mindyangu
heading.backTranslation: Look: The Seed Relationship of Households

body.text: Mbewu leyi hlayisiweke kahle yi va ni matimba ngopfu loko yi tivekile ni loko yi avelaniwa.
body.backTranslation: Seed that is stored well becomes very strong when it is known and when it is shared.

body.text: Languta ndyangu wun'we wu sungula hi ku hlayisa mbewu kahle eka xirimiwa (crop) xin'we. Mbewu yo oma yi nghena eka swikwama leswi tengeke. Swikwama swin'wana swi famba swi ya eka miti leyi nga ekusuhi. Vaakelani va tlherisela hi ku avelana mbewu yo hambana.
body.backTranslation: Look at one family starting by saving seed well from one crop (crop). Dry seed goes into bought packets. Some packets travel to nearby homesteads. Neighbours return by sharing different seed.

body.text: Eku heteleleni, ndyangu wun'wana ni wun'wana wu va ni mixaka yo tala ya mbewu (varieties) ku hundza leyi a wu ri na yona eku sunguleni.
body.backTranslation: In the end, each household has many varieties of seed more than what it had at the beginning.

body.text: Anakanya hi mbewu leyi u nga yi avelanaka ni mbewu leyi u nga yi amukelaka eka muakelani. Mbewu ya famba. Vutivi ni ku tshemba swi fanele swi famba na yona.
body.backTranslation: Think about the seed that you share and the seed that you receive from a neighbour. Seed travels. Knowledge and trust must travel with it.

english.heading: Select Several Parent Plants
body: The largest fruit is not always the best seed parent.
Look at the whole plant.
Was it healthy?
Did it mature at the right time?
Was it true to type?
Save from several good plants, especially in cross-pollinated crops. This prevents the next generation from coming from only one parent.
What would make you reject a seed plant even if its fruit were large?
Go to your own plot. Point out the plants you would select and the plants you would reject. Choose several healthy, true-to-type plants. Reject diseased plants and those that are not true to type.

heading.text: Hlawula Swimilana Swo Tala swa Vatswari

body.text: Mihandzu leyikulu ngopfu a hi yona minkarhi hinkwayo mutswari wa mbewu lowunene.
body.backTranslation: The biggest fruits are not always the good parent of seed.

body.text: Languta ximilana hinkwaxo.
body.backTranslation: Look at the whole plant.

body.text: Xana a xi hanye kahle?
body.backTranslation: Has it lived well/been healthy?

body.text: Xana xi vupfe hi nkarhi lowu faneleke?
body.backTranslation: Did it ripen at the right time?

body.text: Xana a xi fana ni muxaka wa xona (true to type)?
body.backTranslation: Is it like its kind (true to type)?

body.text: Hlayisa mbewu eka swimilana swo tala leswinene, ngopfu-ngopfu eka swirimiwa leswi hlanganaka (cross-pollinated). Leswi swi sivela xitukulwana lexi landzelaka ku huma eka mutswari un'we ntsena.
body.backTranslation: Store seed from many good plants, especially in crops that cross (cross-pollinated). This prevents the next generation from coming from one parent only.

body.text: I yini lexi nga ku endla u ala ximilana xa mbewu, hambiloko mihandzu yi ri leyikulu?
body.backTranslation: What could make you refuse a plant for seed, even if the fruits are big?

body.text: Famba u ya eka ndhawu ya wena yo byala. Komba swimilana leswi u nga swi hlawulaka ni leswi u nga swi alaka. Hlawula swimilana swo tala leswi hanyeke kahle, leswi fanaka ni muxaka wa swona (true to type). Ala leswi vabyaka ni leswi nga fanangiki ni muxaka wa swona.
body.backTranslation: Go to your planting place. Show the plants that you choose and those that you reject. Choose many plants that are alive well, that are like their kind (true to type). Reject those that are sick and those that are not like their kind.

english.heading: Control Pollination
body: Some crops mostly self-pollinate. A small garden can therefore keep the variety similar.
Crops pollinated by wind or insects can cross over long distances.
The distance needed depends on the crop, the place and the purpose of the seed. Do not promise varietal purity until you have checked the crop.
How can you separate two varieties without using distance?
You can plant them at different times so they do not flower together. You can also control pollination by hand or with covers.
Remember the three tools: distance, flowering time or controlled pollination.

heading.text: Lawula Pollination

body.text: Swimilana swin'wana hi ku tala swi endla self-pollination. Hikwalaho ntanga yitsongo yi nga hlayisa muxaka (variety) wu fana.
body.backTranslation: Some plants mostly do self-pollination. Therefore a small garden can/may keep the variety (variety) alike.

body.text: Swimilana leswi pollination ya swona yi endliwaka hi moya kumbe switsotswana swi nga hlangana (cross) hi mpfhuka wo leha.
body.backTranslation: Plants whose pollination is done by wind or insects can/may mix (cross) over a long gap/distance.

body.text: Mpfhuka lowu lavekaka wu ya hi ximilana, ndhawu ni xikongomelo xa mbewu. U nga tshembisi ku tenga ka muxaka (varietal purity) ku se kondza u kambela ximilana.
body.backTranslation: The distance that is needed goes by plant, place and purpose of the seed. Do not promise purity of kind (varietal purity) until you have checked the plant.

body.text: U nga hambanisa mixaka (varieties) yimbirhi hi ndlela yihi handle ko tirhisa mpfhuka?
body.backTranslation: How can you separate two varieties without using distance?

body.text: U nga yi byala hi tinguva to hambana leswaku yi nga vi ni swiluva hi nkarhi wun'we. U nga tlhela u lawula pollination hi voko kumbe hi swifunengeto (covers).
body.backTranslation: You can plant it at different times so that it does not have flowers at one time. You can also control pollination by hand or with coverings (covers).

body.text: Tsundzuka switirhisiwa swinharhu: mpfhuka, nkarhi wa swiluva kumbe pollination leyi lawuriwaka.
body.backTranslation: Remember three tools: gap/distance, time of flowers or pollination that is controlled.

english.heading: Watch: Self-Pollination and Crossing
body: Follow the path of the pollen.
In self-pollination, pollen moves within one flower from the part that produces it to the part that receives it. This often helps the variety remain similar.
In a maize field, wind carries pollen from the tassels to the silks. If two varieties are close together and flower at the same time, they can cross.
Think about how distance or different flowering times could prevent that on your own plot.

heading.text: Languta: Self-Pollination ni Ku Hlangana (crossing)

body.text: Landzelela ndlela ya pollen.
body.backTranslation: Follow the way of pollen.

body.text: Eka self-pollination, pollen yi famba endzeni ka xiluva xin'we, yi suka eka xiphemu lexi xi yi humesaka yi ya eka xiphemu lexi xi yi amukelaka. Minkarhi yo tala leswi swi pfuna muxaka (variety) wu tshama wu fana.
body.backTranslation: In self-pollination, pollen travels inside one flower, it leaves from the part that releases it and goes to the part that receives it. Many times these help the variety (variety) to keep being alike.

body.text: Entangeni ya mavele, moya wu rhwala pollen yi suka eka tassels yi ya eka silks. Loko mixaka (varieties) yimbirhi yi ri ekusuhi ni ku va ni swiluva hi nkarhi wun'we, yi nga hlangana (cross).
body.backTranslation: In the field of maize, wind carries pollen, it leaves from the tassels and goes to the silks. When two varieties (varieties) are nearby and to have flowers at one time, they can/may mix (cross).

body.text: Anakanya hi ndlela leyi mpfhuka kumbe nkarhi wo hambana wa swiluva swi nga swi sivelaka ha yona eka ndhawu ya wena yo byala.
body.backTranslation: Think about how distance or a different flowering time could prevent them in your planting place.

english.heading: Dry and Wet Processing
body: There are two broad ways to process seed.
Dry seed matures in a pod, head or cob. It is collected when fully mature.
Seed inside a fleshy fruit must first be separated from the flesh.
Brief fermentation is especially useful for tomato seed. It is not a rule for every wet-seeded crop.
Think about the crops in your area. Which fit the dry method? Which fit the wet method?
If you have seed or fruit nearby, sort the examples into these two types. Explain the difference by describing what the seed is like at harvest.

heading.text: Ku Lulamisa hi Ndlela yo Oma ni ya Mati
heading.backTranslation: Preparing by the Dry Way and the Water Way

body.text: Ku na tindlela timbirhi leti anameke ta ku lulamisa mbewu.
body.backTranslation: There are two widespread ways of preparing seed.

body.text: Mbewu yo oma yi vupfa eka pod, nhloko kumbe cob. Yi hlengeletiwa loko yi vupfile hi ku helela.
body.backTranslation: Dry seed ripens in the pod, head or cob. It is gathered when it is completely ripe.

body.text: Mbewu leyi nga endzeni ka mihandzu yo tala nyama yi fanele yi sungula yi hambanisiwa ni nyama.
body.backTranslation: Seed that is inside fruits with much flesh must first be separated from the flesh.

body.text: Fermentation ya nkarhi wo koma yi pfuna ngopfu-ngopfu eka mbewu ya tamatisi. A hi nawu eka swimilana hinkwaswo leswi mbewu ya swona yi nga endzeni ka nyama.
body.backTranslation: Short-time fermentation helps especially with tomato seed. It is not a rule for all plants whose seed is inside flesh.

body.text: Anakanya hi swimilana swa le ndhawini ya ka n'wina. Hi swihi leswi fambelanaka ni ndlela yo oma? Hi swihi leswi fambelanaka ni ndlela ya mati?
body.backTranslation: Think about the plants of your area. Which go with the dry way? Which go with the water way?

body.text: Loko u ri ni mbewu kumbe mihandzu ekusuhi, hambanisa swikombiso ku ya hi tinxaka leti timbirhi. Hlamusela ku hambana hi ku hlamusela leswi mbewu yi nga swona hi nkarhi wa ntshovelo.
body.backTranslation: If you have seed or fruits nearby, separate the examples according to the two kinds. Explain the difference by explaining what the seed is at harvest time.

english.heading: Process Dry Seed
body: Leave dry-seeded crops on the plant until the seed is fully mature.
Collect it before weather, birds or bursting pods take the harvest.
Remove chaff and damaged seed.
Then spread the clean seed in a single layer in moving air and shade.
What tells you that dry seed is mature enough to collect?
If you have a dry pod or seed head, handle it. Listen for the seed. Compare green, flexible plant material with brown, brittle material.
Wait for maturity. For final drying, use shade and airflow.

heading.text: Lulamisa Mbewu Yo Oma

body.text: Siya swimilana leswi nga ni mbewu yo oma eka ximilana ku ya fika mbewu yi vupfile hi ku helela.
body.backTranslation: Leave plants that have dry seed on the plant until the seed is completely ripe.

body.text: Yi hlengelete ku nga si va xiyimo xa moya (weather), swinyenyana kumbe ku phaluka ka pods ku teka ntshovelo.
body.backTranslation: Gather it before weather, small birds or the bursting of pods take the harvest.

body.text: Susa chaff ni mbewu leyi onhakeke.
body.backTranslation: Remove chaff and spoiled seed.

body.text: Endzhaku ka sweswo hangalasa mbewu leyi tengeke hi xiyenge xin'we eka moya lowu fambaka ni endzhutini.
body.backTranslation: After that spread the clean seed in one layer in moving air and in shade.

body.text: I yini lexi ku byelaka leswaku mbewu yo oma yi vupfile ku ringana ku hlengeletiwa?
body.backTranslation: What tells you that dry seed is ripe enough to be gathered?

body.text: Loko u ri ni pod yo oma kumbe nhloko ya mbewu, yi khome. Yingisela mbewu. Pimanisa ximilana xa rihlaza lexi bindzukaka ni lexi nga ya buraweni (brown) lexi pasukaka hi ku olova.
body.backTranslation: If you have a dry pod or seed head, hold it. Listen to the seed. Compare a green plant that bends and a brown one that breaks easily.

body.text: Rindza ku vupfa. Eku omiseni ko hetelela, tirhisa ndzhuti ni moya.
body.backTranslation: Wait for ripening. At the final drying, use shade and air.

english.heading: Watch: Dry Processing
body: Allow the seed to mature on the plant before collecting it.
Watch how it is collected once mature. Chaff and debris are removed. Damaged seed is taken out.
The clean seed is then spread in a single layer in moving air and shade.
Follow the steps in order: mature, collect, clean, dry.
Think about where you could carry out each part of this process.

heading.text: Languta: Ku Tirha Mbewu Yo Oma (Dry Processing)

body.text: Pfumelela mbewu yi vupfa eka ximila ku nga si yi hlengeleta.
body.backTranslation: Allow the seed to ripen on the plant before you gather it.

body.text: Languta ndlela leyi yi hlengeletiwaka ha yona loko yi vupfile. Chaff ni debris swa susiwa. Mbewu leyi onhakeke yi susiwa.
body.backTranslation: Look at how it is gathered when it is ripe. Chaff and debris are removed. Spoiled seed is removed.

body.text: Kutani mbewu leyi basileke yi andlariwa hi layer yin'we endzhutini ni le moyeni lowu fambaka.
body.backTranslation: Then the clean seed is spread in a single layer in shade and in moving air.

body.text: Landzelela magoza hi ku landzelelana: vupfa, hlengeleta, basisa, omisa.
body.backTranslation: Follow the steps in order: ripen, gather, clean, dry.

body.text: Anakanyisisa leswaku u nga endla xin'wana ni xin'wana xa swiphemu swa ndlela leyi ndhawini yihi.
body.backTranslation: Think carefully about where you could do each one of the parts of this way.

english.heading: Wet Processing for Tomato Seed
body: Scoop tomato seed and flesh into a clean jar with a little water.
Leave it open or loosely covered. Keep it out of direct sun.
After two to three days, a light film and a sour smell may appear.
Rinse promptly. Remove debris. Then spread the clean seed thinly to dry.
Do not seal an actively fermenting jar.
Think about the signs that tell you the process has begun. Also think about signs that would make you discard the batch.
Find a jar, a sieve and a drying plate. When you are ready, start a small batch. Remember the order: scoop, ferment briefly, rinse and dry completely.

heading.text: Wet Processing ya Mbewu ya Tamatisi

body.text: Susa (scoop) mbewu ni nyama ya tamatisi u swi veka eka jari leyi basileke leyi nga ni mati ntsongo.
body.backTranslation: Remove (scoop) the seed and flesh of the tomato and put them in a clean jar that has a little water.

body.text: Yi siye yi pfulekile kumbe yi funengetiwe kutsongo. Yi sirhelele eka dyambu ra ku kongoma.
body.backTranslation: Leave it open or covered slightly. Protect it from direct sun.

body.text: Endzhaku ka masiku ya 2 ku ya eka 3, xikhumba xo olova ni nun'hwelo lowu bavaka (sour) swi nga humelela.
body.backTranslation: After 2 to 3 days, a soft skin and a sour smell may appear.

body.text: Hlantswa hi ku hatlisa. Susa debris. Kutani andlala mbewu leyi basileke hi layer yin'we leswaku yi oma.
body.backTranslation: Wash quickly. Remove debris. Then spread the clean seed in one layer so that it dries.

body.text: U nga pfali jari leyi ha ku ferment.
body.backTranslation: Do not close the jar that is still fermenting.

body.text: Anakanyisisa hi swikombiso leswi ku tivisaka leswaku endlelo ri sungule. Anakanyisisa na hi swikombiso leswi nga ku endlaka u lahla batch.
body.backTranslation: Think carefully about the signs that tell you that the process has started. Think carefully also about signs that make you discard the batch.

body.text: Kuma jari, sieve ni xibya xo omisa. Loko u lunghekile, sungula batch yo tsongo. Tsundzuka ku landzelelana: susa (scoop), ferment hi nkarhi wo koma, hlantswa u omisa hi ku helela.
body.backTranslation: Get a jar, a sieve and a dish for drying. When you are ready, start with a small batch. Remember the order: remove (scoop), ferment for a short time, wash and dry completely.

english.heading: Watch: Wet Processing for Tomato Seed
body: Watch the whole process in order.
A ripe tomato is opened. The seed and gel are scooped into a clean jar. Only a little water is added.
The jar is left open or loosely covered for two to three days.
When a light film and sour smell appear, the contents are poured through a sieve. The seed is rinsed until it is clean.
Finally, the seed is spread in a single layer in the shade until completely dry.
Repeat the steps to yourself: scoop, ferment briefly, rinse, dry completely.

heading.text: Languta: Wet Processing ya Mbewu ya Tamatisi
heading.backTranslation: Look: Wet Processing of Tomato Seed

body.text: Languta endlelo hinkwaro hi ku landzelelana.
body.backTranslation: Look at the whole process in order.

body.text: Tamatisi leyi vupfeke yi pfuriwa. Mbewu ni gel swi susiwa (scooped) swi vekiwa eka jari leyi basileke. Ku engeteriwa mati ntsongo ntsena.
body.backTranslation: A ripe tomato is opened. The seed and gel are removed (scooped) and put in a clean jar. Only a little water is added.

body.text: Jari yi siyiwa yi pfulekile kumbe yi funengetiwe hi ndlela yo olova 2 ku ya eka 3 wa masiku.
body.backTranslation: The jar is left open or lightly covered for 2 to 3 days.

body.text: Loko xikhumba xo olova ni nun'hwelo lowu bavaka (sour) swi humelela, leswi nga endzeni swi chuhisiwa eka sieve. Mbewu yi hlantswiwa ku kondza yi basa.
body.backTranslation: When a soft skin and a sour smell appear, the contents are drained/poured through a sieve. The seed is washed until it is clean.

body.text: Eku heteleleni, mbewu yi andlariwa hi layer yin'we endzhutini ku kondza yi omile hi ku helela.
body.backTranslation: In the end, the seed is spread in one layer in shade until it is completely dry.

body.text: Tlhela u tivulavule magoza: susa (scoop), ferment hi nkarhi wo koma, hlantswa, omisa hi ku helela.
body.backTranslation: Repeat the steps yourself: remove (scoop), ferment for a short time, wash, dry completely.

english.heading: Practical Activity
body: This is where the lesson leaves the screen and reaches your hands.
Start one real batch of wet-processed seed.
Use one ripe, healthy fruit, a clean jar, a spoon, a little water, a sieve and a drying plate.
Put the seed, flesh and a little water into the jar. Add a label with the date.
You will look after this jar after the lesson. Decide now when you will inspect it, when you will rinse it and when you will dry the seed.
Your jar needs a date and a return plan. Write down the date when you will inspect it after two days.

heading.text: Ntirho wo Endla

body.text: Laha dyondzo yi huma eka skrini yi fika emavokweni ya wena.
body.backTranslation: Here the lesson comes out of the screen and arrives in your hands.

body.text: Sungula batch yin'we ya xiviri ya mbewu leyi lulamisiweke hi wet processing.
body.backTranslation: Start one real batch of seed prepared by wet processing.

body.text: Tirhisa muhandzu wun'we lowu vupfeke, lowu hanyaka kahle, jari leyi basileke, spuni, mati ntsongo, sieve ni xibya xo omisa.
body.backTranslation: Use one ripe, healthy fruit, a clean jar, a spoon, a little water, a sieve and a drying dish.

body.text: Veka mbewu, nyama ni mati ntsongo eka jari. Namarhela label leyi nga ni siku.
body.backTranslation: Put seed, flesh and a little water in the jar. Stick on a label that has the date.

body.text: U ta khathalela jari leyi endzhaku ka dyondzo. Hlawula sweswi leswaku u ta yi kambela rini, u ta yi hlantswa rini ni leswaku u ta omisa mbewu rini.
body.backTranslation: You will look after the jar after the lesson. Decide now when you will check it, when you will wash it and when you will dry the seed.

body.text: Jari ya wena yi lava siku ni kungu ra ku tlhelela. Tsala siku leri u nga ta yi kambela ha rona endzhaku ka 2 wa masiku.
body.backTranslation: Your jar needs a date and an intention to return. Write the date on which you will check it after 2 days.

english.heading: Dry First, Seal Later
body: Drying is not a decorative final step.
Moist seed keeps breathing. It can heat, rot or die in storage.
Use shade, moving air and time.
Seal seed only when you are sure it is dry.
Which place in your home has shade and airflow, but is protected from rain and cooking steam?
Choose one safe drying place. Then identify one unsafe place.
Repeat this to check your understanding: dry first, seal later.

heading.text: Sungula U Omisa, Endzhaku U Pfala

body.text: Ku omisa a hi goza ro hetelela ro sasekisa.
body.backTranslation: Drying is not a final decorative step.

body.text: Mbewu leyi tsakameke yi ya emahlweni yi hefemula. Yi nga hisa, yi bola kumbe yi fa loko yi hlayisiwa.
body.backTranslation: Damp seed goes on breathing. It can heat up, rot or die when it is stored.

body.text: Tirhisa ndzhuti, moya lowu fambaka ni nkarhi.
body.backTranslation: Use shade, moving air and time.

body.text: Pfala mbewu ntsena loko u tiyiseke leswaku yi omile.
body.backTranslation: Close the seed only when you are sure that it is dry.

body.text: I ndhawu yihi ekaya ra wena leyi nga ni ndzhuti ni moya, kambe yi sirheleriwaka eka mpfula ni hunguva (steam) ya ku sweka?
body.backTranslation: Which place at your home has shade and air, but is protected from rain and steam from cooking?

body.text: Hlawula ndhawu yin'we leyi hlayisekeke yo omisa. Kutani kuma ndhawu yin'we leyi nga hlayisekangiki.
body.backTranslation: Choose one place that is safe for drying. Then find one place that is not safe.

body.text: Phindha leswi ku kambela leswaku u swi twisisa: sungula u omisa, endzhaku u pfala.
body.backTranslation: Repeat these to check that you understand: first dry, afterwards close.

english.heading: Protect Seed from Heat, Light and Moisture
body: Paper packets breathe and organise seed. But they are not enough in a humid climate.
Once the seed is completely dry, place the labelled packets inside a sealed, moisture-proof container. If available, include a food-safe desiccant.
Keep the container as cool and dark as possible in your home.
Which room or cupboard in your home stays coolest and driest?
Compare a paper envelope on its own with an envelope inside a sealed container.
Safe storage has two layers: a labelled paper packet inside a dry, sealed container.

heading.text: Sirhelela Mbewu eka Ku Hisa, Ku Vonakala ni Ku Tsakama
heading.backTranslation: Protect Seed from Heat, Light and Dampness

body.text: Swikwama swa phepha swa hefemula naswona swi hlela mbewu. Kambe a swi eneli endhawini leyi tsakameke swinene (humid climate).
body.backTranslation: Paper packets breathe and they organise seed. But they are not enough in a very damp place (humid climate).

body.text: Loko mbewu yi omile hi ku helela, veka swikwama leswi nga ni label endzeni ka xibya lexi pfaleke lexi sirhelelaka eka ku tsakama. Loko yi kona, engetela desiccant leyi nga riki ni khombo eka swakudya.
body.backTranslation: When the seed is completely dry, put the bags that have labels inside a closed dish that protects against dampness. If available, add a desiccant that has no danger to food.

body.text: Hlayisa xibya lexi xi pholile ni ku va ni munyama hilaha swi kotekaka hakona ekaya.
body.backTranslation: Keep the dish cool and dark as far as is possible at home.

body.text: I kamara kumbe khabodo yihi ekaya leyi tshamaka yi pholile ni yo omisa swinene?
body.backTranslation: Which room or cupboard at home stays cool and very dry?

body.text: Fananisa envulopo ya phepha ntsena ni envulopo leyi nga endzeni ka xibya lexi pfaleke.
body.backTranslation: Compare a paper envelope only and an envelope that is inside a closed container.

body.text: Vuhlayiselo lebyi hlayisekeke byi na swiphemu swimbirhi: xikwama xa phepha lexi nga ni label endzeni ka xibya lexi omeke, lexi pfaleke.
body.backTranslation: Safe storage has two parts: a paper bag with a label inside a dry, closed container.

english.heading: Label Every Packet
body: Storage protects the seed physically. Written information protects its meaning.
The packet must tell the next person what crop it is.
It must give the variety or local name.
It must say when the seed was saved and where it came from.
Which local names could be lost if you write only the crop name?
Take a blank packet. Practise writing the four pieces of information: crop, variety or local name, date and source.
Check again that all four are present.

heading.text: Label Xikwama Xin'wana ni Xin'wana

body.text: Vuhlayiselo byi sirhelela miri wa mbewu. Mahungu lama tsariweke ma sirhelela nhlamuselo ya yona.
body.backTranslation: Storage protects the body of the seed. Written information protects its description.

body.text: Xikwama xi fanele ku byela munhu la landzelaka leswaku i xirimiwa xihi.
body.backTranslation: The bag must tell the next person which crop it is.

body.text: Xi fanele ku nyika muxaka (variety) kumbe vito leri tirhisiwaka endhawini.
body.backTranslation: It must give the variety or the name that is used locally.

body.text: Xi fanele ku vula leswaku mbewu yi hlayisiwe rini ni leswaku yi humile kwihi.
body.backTranslation: It must say when the seed was stored and where it came from.

body.text: Xana i mavito yihi ya le ndhawini lama nga ta lahleka loko u tsala vito ra xirimiwa ntsena?
body.backTranslation: What local names could be lost when you write only the name of the crop?

body.text: Teka xikwama lexi nga tsariwangiki nchumu. Dyondza ku tsala swiphemu swa mahungu swa 4: xirimiwa, muxaka (variety) kumbe vito leri tirhisiwaka endhawini, siku ni ndhawu leyi yi humeke eka yona.
body.backTranslation: Take a bag that has nothing written on it. Learn to write 4 pieces of information: crop, variety or the name used locally, date and the place from which it came.

body.text: Kambela nakambe leswaku hinkwaswo swa 4 swi kona.
body.backTranslation: Check again that all 4 are there.

english.heading: Ten-Seed Germination Test
body: A seed packet can look perfect even when the seed is losing life.
Ten seeds make the calculation easy.
Keep them warm and moist. Do not submerge them in water.
Then count the normal seedlings.
Six out of ten is about sixty percent. That tells you to sow more heavily, use the seed only as a trial, or replace it.
If eight seeds out of ten germinate, what percentage is that?
The answer is eighty percent.
Start a ten-seed test with an old packet. Write down the date and the day when you will count.

heading.text: Germination Test ya Mbewu ya 10

body.text: Xikwama xa mbewu xi nga vonaka xi hetisekile hambi mbewu yi lahlekeriwa hi vutomi.
body.backTranslation: A bag of seed can look complete even if the seed has lost life.

body.text: Mbewu ya 10 yi endla ku hlayela ku olova.
body.backTranslation: 10 seeds make easy counting.

body.text: Yi hlayise yi kufumela naswona yi tsakama. U nga yi nghenisi ematini hi ku helela.
body.backTranslation: Keep them covered and damp. Do not put them completely in water.

body.text: Kutani hlayela swimilana leswi tolovelekeke (normal seedlings).
body.backTranslation: Then count the normal plants (normal seedlings).

body.text: 6 eka 10 i ku fana ni 60 wa tiphesente. Leswi swi ku byela ku byala mbewu yo tala ku tlula leswi tolovelekeke, ku tirhisa mbewu ntsena tanihi ku ringeta, kumbe ku yi cincisa.
body.backTranslation: 6 out of 10 is equal to 60 percent. This tells you to plant more seed than usual, to use the seed only as a test, or to swap it.

body.text: Loko mbewu ya 8 eka 10 yi mila, i phesente yingani?
body.backTranslation: If 8 seeds out of 10 germinate, what percent is it?

body.text: Nhlamulo i 80 wa tiphesente.
body.backTranslation: The answer is 80 percent.

body.text: Sungula germination test ya mbewu ya 10 hi xikwama xa khale. Tsala siku ra sweswi ni siku leri u nga ta hlayela ha rona.
body.backTranslation: Start a germination test of 10 seeds with an old bag. Write today's date and the date on which you will count.

english.heading: Watch: Ten-Seed Germination Test
body: Count exactly ten seeds.
Place them in two rows of five.
Keep them on moist paper or cloth. Do not submerge them in water.
After some time, count again.
Here, six have germinated. Four have not. The total is still ten.
The germination rate is therefore sixty percent.
Check yourself. Did you count ten at the start, six germinated seeds and four ungerminated seeds at the end?

heading.text: Languta: Germination Test ya Mbewu ya 10

body.text: Hlayela mbewu ya 10 hi ku hetiseka.
body.backTranslation: Count 10 seeds completely.

body.text: Yi veke hi tirhowu ta 2, yin'wana ni yin'wana yi ni 5.
body.backTranslation: Place them in 2 rows, each with 5.

body.text: Yi hlayise ehenhla ka phepha kumbe lapi leri tsakamaka. U nga yi nghenisi ematini.
body.backTranslation: Keep them on top of a damp paper or cloth. Do not put them in water.

body.text: Endzhaku ka nkarhi, hlayela nakambe.
body.backTranslation: After a time, count again.

body.text: Laha, 6 yi mile. 4 a yi mila. Nhlayo hinkwayo yi ha ri 10.
body.backTranslation: Here, 6 have germinated. 4 did not germinate. The total is still 10.

body.text: Mpimo wa ku mila hikokwalaho i 60 wa tiphesente.
body.backTranslation: The germination measure is therefore 60 percent.

body.text: Tivutise. Xana u hlayele 10 eku sunguleni, mbewu ya 6 leyi mileke ni mbewu ya 4 leyi nga mila eku heteleleni?
body.backTranslation: Ask yourself. Did you count 10 at the beginning, 6 seeds that germinated and 4 seeds that did not germinate at the end?

english.heading: Share Seed with Its Information
body: A seed exchange is not a table of unknown packets.
A good exchange moves information with the seed.
It tells you what the seed is. Where it came from. When it was saved. And whether it has been tested.
This honesty strengthens the whole network.
What information would help you trust seed from another household?
Take one of your packets. Practise describing it before sharing it. Give the seed and its basic history together.

heading.text: Avelana Mbewu Ni Mahungu Ya Yona

body.text: Ku cincisana mbewu a hi tafula ra swikwama leswi nga tivekiki.
body.backTranslation: Exchanging seed is not a table of unknown bags.

body.text: Ku cincisana kuhle ku fambisa mahungu swin'we ni mbewu.
body.backTranslation: Good exchanging moves information together with seed.

body.text: Ku ku byela leswaku mbewu i yini. Yi humile kwihi. Yi hlayisiwe rini. Ni leswaku xana yi kambeliwile (tested).
body.backTranslation: It tells you what the seed is. Where it came from. When it was stored. And whether it has been tested (tested).

body.text: Ku tshembeka loku ku tiyisa vuxaka hinkwabyo (network).
body.backTranslation: This trustworthiness strengthens the whole relationship (network).

body.text: Hi byihi vuxokoxoko lebyi nga ku pfunaka ku tshemba mbewu leyi humaka eka ndyangu wun'wana?
body.backTranslation: Which details help you trust seed that comes from another household?

body.text: Teka xin'wana xa swikwama swa wena. Dyondza ku xi hlamusela u nga se xi avelana. Nyika mbewu ni matimu ya yona ya masungulo swin'we.
body.backTranslation: Take one of your bags. Learn to explain it before it is shared. Give the seed together with its original history.

english.heading: Field Assignment
body: This task is small enough to finish. It is important enough to matter.
Build one working seed-storage container.
Put labelled paper packets inside a dry, sealed container.
Take a photograph of it.
Then name the crop whose seed you will save this season.
The photograph is evidence. The packet is a beginning.
What do you still need to finish this at home?
Write a short materials list. Choose a completion date.

Before sealing the container, check your work: the seed is completely dry; every packet has the crop, variety and date; the container is cool, dark and protected from moisture; and you selected several healthy parent plants.

heading.text: Ntirho wa Nsimu

body.text: Ntirho lowu wu ntsongo lerova wu nga hetiwa. Wu ni nkoka lowu eneleke.
body.backTranslation: This task is small so that it can be finished. It has enough value.

body.text: Aka xibya xin'we xa ku hlayisa mbewu lexi tirhaka.
body.backTranslation: Build one working seed-storage container.

body.text: Veka swikwama swa phepha leswi nga ni label eka xibya lexi omeke, lexi pfaleke.
body.backTranslation: Put paper bags that have labels in a dry, closed container.

body.text: Teka xifaniso xa xona.
body.backTranslation: Take a picture of it.

body.text: Kutani vula xirimiwa lexi u nga ta hlayisa mbewu ya xona nkarhi lowu.
body.backTranslation: Then name the crop whose seed you will store this time.

body.text: Xifaniso i vumbhoni. Xikwama i masungulo.
body.backTranslation: The picture is evidence. The bag is the beginning.

body.text: Hi yini leswi u ha swi lavaka leswaku u heta ntirho lowu ekaya?
body.backTranslation: What do you still need in order to finish this task at home?

body.text: Tsala nxaxamelo wo koma wa swilo leswi lavekaka. Hlawula siku ra ku heta.
body.backTranslation: Write a short list of the things that are needed. Choose a finishing date.

body.text: U nga se pfala xibya, kambela ntirho wa wena: mbewu yi omile hi ku helela; xikwama xin'wana ni xin'wana xi na xirimiwa, muxaka (variety) ni siku; xibya xi pholile, xi ni munyama, xi sirheleriwile eka ku tsakama; u hlawule swimila swo hlayanyana swa vatswari leswi hanyaka kahle.
body.backTranslation: Before you close the container, check your work: the seed is completely dry; each bag has the crop, variety and date; the container is cool, dark, protected from dampness; you have chosen a few healthy parent plants.

english.heading: Field Action
body: Select.
Process.
Protect.
Verify.
Those four actions carry a seed collection from this field into the next season.
Begin with one crop and do it well.
Which crop will you begin with?
Say it aloud. Then choose one action you will take next.
The next season is already inside the seed you choose today.

heading.text: Goza ra Nsimu

body.text: Hlawula.
body.backTranslation: Choose.

body.text: Lulamisa (process).
body.backTranslation: Prepare (process).

body.text: Sirhelela.
body.backTranslation: Protect.

body.text: Tiyisisa.
body.backTranslation: Confirm.

body.text: Swiendlo leswi swa 4 swi rhwala nhlengeletano ya mbewu ku suka ensin'wini lowu, swi yi yisa eka nkarhi lowu landzelaka.
body.backTranslation: These 4 actions carry the seed collection from this field, taking it to the next time.

body.text: Sungula hi xirimiwa xin'we u xi endla kahle.
body.backTranslation: Start with one crop and do it well.

body.text: U ta sungula hi xirimiwa xihi?
body.backTranslation: Which crop will you start with?

body.text: Xi vule hi rito leri tlakukeke. Kutani hlawula goza rin'we leri u nga ta ri teka endzhaku.
body.backTranslation: Say it with a raised voice. Then choose one step that you will take afterwards.

body.text: Nkarhi lowu landzelaka wu se wu ri endzeni ka mbewu leyi u yi hlawulaka namuntlha.
body.backTranslation: The next time will already be inside the seed that you choose today.
